tier_reason: First-party README tables against GEOS 3.13.1 (Shapely 2.1.2) over 26 parcel workloads, with a public harness (tests/compare/run.py and probes.py, documented in tests/compare/README.md) and Zig 0.16.0 with -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe stated. The machine is described only as 'one idle machine' with no CPU model, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Union table (median of three suite runs of 11 repeats): 4,040 parcels qdgeo wasm 160 ms, qdgeo native 130 ms vs GEOS 426 ms; 1,000 parcels 20.3 / 16.8 ms vs 65.7 ms. Derived from page data: 2.7x (wasm) and 3.3x (native) on the full union; the README's Design goals section rounds this to '3.1x native GEOS'. Geometric mean over the 26 workloads: GEOS native 1.5x slower than qdgeo wasm (range across runs 1.36-1.62). Buffer of 100 parcels +2 m: 1.30 ms vs GEOS 4.54 ms. GEOS is faster on the single 19,208-coordinate parcel buffer (+2 m 8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms; -2 m 13.0 ms vs 31.9 ms).
corrections.caveats: Application-level comparison, and the README admits the boundaries are not equal. GEOS gets shapely.union_all over geometries that are already GEOS objects (no parse or encode), while qdgeo native rows include a WKB parse/encode round trip and the wasm rows a flat-ABI copy. That favors GEOS, though GEOS is native and qdgeo wasm is not. The harness notes GEOS measured 417 ms and 356 ms for the same workload an hour apart, and the README says to treat gaps under 20% as unresolved. GEOS is faster on very large single polygons. The shipped build keeps safety checks (ReleaseSafe; ReleaseFast is 11% faster). qdgeo rejects invalid input instead of repairing it, and it errors on 4 of 3,946 valid cluster unions it cannot node exactly. The project is days old (first commit 2026-09-14), only one dataset (GeoMoose parcels) is tested, and it is not a general GEOS replacement. The CPU model is missing, so tier C.

notes: Every number in the record matches the README tables. The '3.1x' headline does not exactly match the table, which gives 2.7x for wasm and 3.3x for native, so I spelled out the derived ratios. Metadata from github.com: MIT (LICENSE.txt and package.json), 0 stars, 15 commits, first commit 2026-09-14, last commit 2026-09-23. The JTS test cases bundled under tests/jts are EDL-1.0, test data only.

tier_reason: The README Performance table is a first-party run against imbcmdth's old RTree on Node.js v6.2.2 on a mid-2012 Retina MacBook Pro, with no CPU model. The script it cites (debug/perf.js, now bench/perf.js) times only RBush, so the old-RTree column cannot be reproduced from the repo: C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Node.js v6.2.2. The README cites debug/perf.js; that path is gone, and the current bench/perf.js (npm run perf) times only RBush, not the old RTree.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are from Node 6.2.2 on a 2012 laptop and compare against an old JavaScript R-tree (imbcmdth/RTree), not a C/C++ library or Boost.Geometry. The benchmark script the README names now lives at bench/perf.js and runs RBush alone, so the baseline column cannot be reproduced from the repo. The CPU model is missing. The table predates RBush v4. The baseline is another R-tree implementation, so this shows algorithm tuning (R*-tree split, OMT bulk load) rather than a win over a major incumbent. Some README ratios are rounded loosely (remove: 1.18 s vs 0.02 s is about 59x on the page data, printed as 50x).

notes: Every number in the record matches the README Performance table verbatim. Metadata from github.com: MIT (LICENSE file and package.json), 2.8k stars, 301 commits, last commit 2026-04-03 ('update dev deps'), not a fork or archived. The last functional release was v4.0.1 (Aug 2024).
